notes: Texas localization of the civic-leadership legacy model — the edition of the bridge: Willie L. Brown Jr. was born in Mineola, Texas (1934), and the model's eleventh principle ('From segregated Mineola to San Francisco State: education as the bridge across barriers') begins here. DISCLAIMER, carried from the app: this track is a proposal built from the Willie L. Brown Jr. Institute of Politics and Public Service's public mission and the Fellowship Program at San Francisco State University. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or reviewed by the Institute, SF State, or Mayor Brown. 5 tracks x 10 themes x 5 grade bands = 250 blocks. Expanded by tools/generate_pack.py.

tracks.name: The bridge from Mineola: service as a way out and a way back

themes.description: The founding story taught honestly — a segregated East Texas schoolroom, a train west, and education as the bridge across barriers that still stand.
themes.transfer_check: Research the schooling actually available in one Texas town in the 1940s and compare it, with evidence, to the same town today.

themes.theme: Service as a craft, not a slogan
themes.description: Public service with roles, crews, evidence and credentials — every course ending before a real audience.
themes.transfer_check: Complete one documented act of public service in your county and present it to a real audience beyond your classroom.

themes.theme: The public servants two streets away
themes.description: Mapping who serves within reach — the county clerk, the librarian, the volunteer firefighter, the extension agent.
themes.transfer_check: Interview one working public servant about a typical day and present their real duties against what you had assumed.

themes.theme: Who is missing from the room
themes.description: Inclusion as a design decision: reading any civic room for who is absent and naming the barrier that kept them out.
themes.transfer_check: Observe one real public meeting and report who was present, who was affected but absent, and one barrier that plausibly explains it.

themes.theme: The placement inside a real agency
themes.description: Shadow days, junior placements and supervised hours inside county offices, libraries and public programs, at every age.
themes.transfer_check: Complete a placement, shadow day or structured volunteer shift with a real public body, confirmed by a supervisor.

themes.description: The weekly cohort habit — field experience brought back to a circle that questions it.
themes.transfer_check: Run or take a speaking role in a seminar circle on a live local issue, presenting field evidence and taking questions.

themes.description: Being mentored by someone ahead and mentoring someone behind, with the leader's-story interview as a core text.
themes.transfer_check: Record a leader's-story interview with an experienced public servant or elder, and lead one session passing a skill to a younger learner.

themes.description: First-generation pathways and the blocked door as history, law and practice in Texas — with the debate included, not avoided.
themes.transfer_check: Research one Texan who broke a civic ceiling, and identify one barrier data shows still standing in your county, with the numbers.

themes.description: The service ledger — hours, artifacts, references, credentials — as a portfolio that opens doors.
themes.transfer_check: Assemble your own service ledger to date in a form a scholarship or employer could verify.

themes.theme: The on-ramp: from county seat to public life
themes.description: The grade-12 pathways into Texas public service — public-affairs programs, civil service, the first paid public job.
themes.transfer_check: Map three real next-step routes into Texas public service — requirements, deadlines, first application step completed or drafted.

tracks.name: The county: two hundred and fifty-four courthouses

themes.description: Texas's 254 counties — why so many, what a county is actually responsible for, and where yours sits.
themes.transfer_check: Produce the one-page profile of your own county — population, seat, governing bodies, three services it actually runs — from official sources.

themes.description: The county judge and four commissioners — the court that is not a court, and what it decides every Tuesday.
themes.transfer_check: Attend or watch one real commissioners court meeting and report one decision, who voted how, and who it affects.

themes.theme: The elected row: sheriff, clerk, tax assessor-collector
themes.description: Texas's long ballot of county officers — sheriff, clerks, assessor-collector, constables, justices of the peace — each answering to voters.
themes.transfer_check: List your county's actual elected officers by name and office, and explain one real recent decision each made that touched residents.

themes.theme: The school district and the board
themes.description: Independent school districts as the education government — boards, superintendents, bond elections and the meeting that sets your school's fate.
themes.transfer_check: Attend or watch one real school board meeting in your district and report one decision made and its effect.

themes.theme: The special districts nobody can name
themes.description: MUDs, groundwater districts, hospital and appraisal districts — the boards that tax and decide, largely unwatched.
themes.transfer_check: Identify three special districts covering your own address, and for one find its board, budget and next public meeting.

themes.theme: The property tax and the appraisal
themes.description: Where county money comes from — the appraisal, the rate hearings, the homestead exemption — and protesting a valuation properly.
themes.transfer_check: Read one real appraisal notice, verify its facts, and file or fully draft the protest the rules allow.

themes.theme: The permit, the complaint, the record
themes.description: The resident's three transactions — asking permission, reporting a problem, requesting a record under the Public Information Act.
themes.transfer_check: Complete one real county or city transaction (permit lookup, service request, or public-information request) and document the outcome.

themes.description: The Open Meetings Act, the sign-up sheet, the three minutes — speaking to a Texas body so it enters the record.
themes.transfer_check: Deliver (or fully rehearse to the real rules) a public comment to a local body on a live agenda item, structured for the record.

themes.theme: City and county: who does what
themes.description: Home-rule cities, general-law towns and the unincorporated county — the services that switch at the city limit.
themes.transfer_check: For your own address, produce the who-fixes-what card: five common problems matched to the correct government and office.

themes.description: Escalation above the county — state oversight, the attorney general's opinions, the courts and the press.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real or case-study county failure and map its escalation ladder in order, drafting the first escalation document.

themes.theme: The capitol and the two chambers
themes.description: The Texas House and Senate, districts and leadership — and the Lieutenant Governor's unusual power over the Senate's agenda.
themes.transfer_check: Identify your actual state representative and senator by district lookup and summarise one bill each has authored recently.

themes.theme: One hundred and forty days, every other year
themes.description: The biennial regular session and the special sessions only the Governor can call — why the calendar shapes everything.
themes.transfer_check: Find the most recent session's actual dates and explain, with one real example, what the compressed calendar did to a bill.

themes.description: Filing, committee, calendars, the floor, the other chamber, the Governor's desk — following one real bill, including where bills die.
themes.transfer_check: Track one real bill from the last session through each stage on the Legislature's own site and state where it stalled or how it passed.

themes.theme: The committee room is the real floor
themes.description: Testimony, substitutes and the calendar committees — where bills actually live and die, and the citizen's chair at the table.
themes.transfer_check: Watch one real committee hearing (live or archived) and report the arguments, amendments and vote as the record shows.

themes.theme: The budget the state must balance
themes.description: The biennial budget, the comptroller's revenue estimate and the rainy-day fund — how Texas money is actually decided.
themes.transfer_check: From official documents, chart the state's five largest spending areas and follow one down to a program in your county.

themes.theme: The agencies that carry out the words
themes.description: Agencies, boards and the administrative code — how a passed law becomes a rule, a form and an inspector, and sunset review's regular reckoning.
themes.transfer_check: Pick one state rule that touches your life, find it in the administrative code, and trace it to the statute that authorised it.

themes.description: The routes from resident to lawmaking — contacting members, registering a position, testifying, and the idea that becomes a filed bill.
themes.transfer_check: Draft a one-page bill proposal on a real local problem and deliver it (or rehearsed testimony for it) in proper form.

themes.description: Texas's twin high courts — Supreme Court and Court of Criminal Appeals — and how an ordinary case climbs to either.
themes.transfer_check: Map one real Texas case's path from filing to final ruling, naming each court correctly.

themes.description: Texas's long constitution and the amendment elections — reading the propositions before voting on them.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real past or pending amendment, translate its ballot language into plain words, and present the strongest case each way.

themes.description: Coalitions in a chamber where the calendar is the weapon — counting before the vote, and consensus that tolerates opposing ideas.
themes.transfer_check: For one real close vote, reconstruct the coalition: who moved, what they traded, and how the count was made.

themes.description: Who may vote in Texas, the registration deadline, and the habit of checking your own record before it matters.
themes.transfer_check: Verify a real registration (yours or a consenting adult's) through the state's official portal and correct any detail found wrong.

themes.description: Texas's open primaries, the majority-vote runoff, and reading which contest actually decides your district.
themes.transfer_check: For two offices on a real ballot, explain the rules that currently govern each and identify which stage effectively decides the seat.

themes.theme: The ID at the polling place
themes.description: The identification rules as they currently stand, the declaration alternative, and helping a voter arrive prepared.
themes.transfer_check: Build the document checklist for three different real voters against the current official rules, citing the Secretary of State.

themes.description: Judges, school boards, bond propositions and MUD elections — the down-ballot lines that move your money and your block.
themes.transfer_check: Obtain your actual sample ballot for a real election and produce a plain-language guide for every line below the top race.

themes.description: Texas's two-week early window, countywide vote centers where they exist, and mail ballots for those who qualify.
themes.transfer_check: Build the complete voting plan for two different real voters — one straightforward, one facing a barrier such as mobility or work hours.

themes.description: Election judges, clerks and poll watchers — the trained neighbours who run the machinery, and how to become one.
themes.transfer_check: Find your county's actual requirements and application to serve as an election worker and submit or fully prepare it.

themes.description: Campaign finance disclosure and the Ethics Commission — following the money in one real race through the public filings.
themes.transfer_check: Pull the actual campaign finance filings for one recent local race and report its top contributors and spending, with sources.

themes.description: Petitions, coalitions and the packed courthouse — moving an issue between elections, counting votes before the vote.
themes.transfer_check: Organize or fully plan an issue campaign for one concrete local change: the decision-maker, the coalition map, the count you need.

themes.description: Election misinformation in Texas's channels — the claims that recur, and the official sources that settle them.
themes.transfer_check: Fact-check three circulating election claims against the Secretary of State and county officials' records and publish the corrected version.

themes.description: Canvass, certification, recounts and contests — how results become final and what a citizen can lawfully question.
themes.transfer_check: Trace one real Texas race from election night to certified result, naming each step and any challenge lodged.

tracks.name: Storm, grid and the long border of water

themes.description: Hurricane coast, tornado alley, flash-flood hills and drought plains — Texas's hazard map as its civic agenda.
themes.transfer_check: Map the hazards that shape your own county — surge zones, floodplains, drought status — from official sources.

themes.description: Watches, warnings, evacuation zones and the lessons written by Harvey and Rita — the governance of leaving the coast.
themes.transfer_check: Build a coastal household's hurricane plan against the county's actual guidance — zone, route, trigger, destination — and rehearse the leave decision.

themes.description: ERCOT's separate grid, the winter of Uri, and what a household and a block do when the power market fails.
themes.transfer_check: Prepare a real household for a multi-day outage in heat and in cold — essentials, medical needs, neighbours checked — and run a drill.

themes.description: Flash floods and reservoir releases — reading the floodplain map, the low-water crossing rule, and insurance that actually covers water.
themes.transfer_check: Read your address's actual flood zone, state the action sequence for a warning at three lead times, and check what a real policy covers.

themes.description: Groundwater districts, the rule of capture and the shrinking aquifers — water law as neighbourhood politics.
themes.transfer_check: Trace your own water to its source, name the district that governs it, and summarise one live decision before that district.

themes.description: The deadliest weather — who heat kills, the cooling-center map, and the checking list two doors away.
themes.transfer_check: Write and rehearse a heat-emergency plan for a real household including one vulnerable neighbour's specific arrangements.

themes.theme: The border of water and the working coast
themes.description: Ports, petrochemicals, fisheries and the Gulf — the anchor industries on the water and the arguments they generate.
themes.transfer_check: Profile one real water-dependent industry site near your region: its jobs and taxes, its permits, and one live controversy from both sides.

themes.description: CERT teams, church networks and the truck-and-chainsaw culture — organized so help helps.
themes.transfer_check: Complete or map enrolment in one recognised local response group, and build the (consented) support map for one street.

themes.description: After the storm — FEMA, the GLO programs, insurance and elevation — and why the same event lands unequally.
themes.transfer_check: From one documented Texas disaster, chart the recovery programs and identify, with evidence, one group the paperwork left behind.

themes.description: The capstone: civic leadership where storm, grid and water are all in motion — weighing protection, retreat and cost with real neighbours in the room.
themes.transfer_check: Run or present a structured deliberation on one real local resilience decision — options, trade-offs, affected voices — and deliver the recommendation you would defend in public.
